newsitem.title: UK: U.S. bonds could outpace Europe as rates put on hold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bonds could outpace Europe as rates put on hold.

text.p: U.S. government bonds could outpace Europe after the Federal Reserve's decision to leave interest rates on hold, but investors will have to hurry as the same old rate worries will soon return, analysts said on Wednesday.

Ten-year Treasuries or T-notes are likely to outperform German Bunds in the short-term, but markets will be fixed squarely on economic data and the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on July 1 and 2.
On Tuesday the Fed left the key federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent.

"The focus in the U.S. now is just immediately on the July FOMC and on the likelihood of a strong payroll figure at the beginning of June," said Kit Juckes, head of bond and currency strategy at NatWest Capital Markets in London, adding that the market was left with a pretty solid conviction that rates are set to go up.
Treasuries closed solidly higher in New York on Tuesday after the meeting and they outpaced Bunds in early European trade on Wednesday.

The 10-year T-note/Bund gap -- which reflects the premium at which U.S. Treasuries trade over German Bunds -- had slimmed to 100 basis points by 0719 GMT, compared with 104 basis points at the close of business on Tuesday.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, said the spread could pull in to around 90 basis points near term.
"We've now got a breathing space until the July meeting," he said. "I don't think the outperformance is going to be too major as I don't think there's going to be too much poor news for Bunds."
The market is waiting to see if April's slow-down in growth was more than just a pause, Edmonds said.
"I wouldn't expect markets to react too dramatically until it is confirmed growth is at a sustainable pace."
But Juckes at NatWest said that in the longer term, data would show the U.S. economy continuing at a pace that would unnerve bond markets.

"It would be amazing if that was the last rate rise," he said. "The U.S. economy is like a car on a downhill slope without the brakes on. Unless you put something in its way it's not going to slow down on its own."
The Fed raised its federal funds target rate to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent on March 25.
Juckes expected the T-note/Bund gap to widen toward the 130 basis point level longer term.
"We will only go out slowly becasue there is a fair amount of demand on the part of international investors," he said.
But David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London, expected all bond markets to gain from the Fed's cautious strategy.

"The Fed is making quite a clear statement it's not going to get into the successive rate hike mode they were in 1994," he said. "It is moving cautiously and gradually here and is very mindful about the markets' response," he said.
